concept.name: Equity index future
concept.definition: A standardized, exchange-traded futures contract on a stock index — such as the S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100 — that provides cash-settled exposure to the index level without holding any of the constituent stocks.
concept.intuition: An equity index future is the whole stock market in one leveraged ticket: you gain or lose the index's move times a fixed multiplier, cash-settled, with no shares ever changing hands.
concept.mechanics: Contract value equals the index level times a fixed multiplier (e.g., $50 per index point for the E-mini S&P 500). Positions are margined and marked to market daily, trade nearly around the clock, and settle in cash to the index value at expiry; rolling from one quarterly expiry to the next maintains continuous exposure.
concept.formula: Contract notional = index level x multiplier (e.g., E-mini S&P 500: $50 x index level).
concept.failure_modes: Leverage magnifies losses, and prices can gap outside cash-market hours, so positions move when the underlying stock market is closed. Rolling expiring contracts incurs basis costs, and index concentration means a handful of large constituents can dominate the exposure.
concept.misconceptions: That an index future holds the underlying stocks — it is pure cash-settled price exposure with no ownership, dividends, or voting rights. Also, the futures price is not a forecast of where the index will be; it reflects spot plus financing minus expected dividends.
concept.example: Buying one E-mini S&P 500 future at an index level of 6,000 controls $300,000 of exposure; a 100-point index rise earns 100 x $50 = $5,000.
